I've got all three, and they each have their benefits.

  • Windows

I've been using Windows on desktop and server for over two decades. In a nutshell: "For some stuff, you still don't have a choice." Some software is only available on Windows.

I use Win7, having avoided 8 and 10 on general principle. The UI of 8 would only make life more difficult, and as a previous user of Windows CE and Windows Mobile, Microsoft trying to ram it's tablet and phone crap down my throat via my desktop only serves to piss me off. Windows 10 I'm not interested in until it matures (like most Microsoft products, never touch an x.0 release) and until they sort out the obvious privacy flaws. Even then, I don't see it would bring me any real benefit. And this is from someone who genuinely still believes that Vista was a massive and much needed upgrade from XP.

The Windows ecosystem's greatest advantage is compatibility, and the fact that the vast majority of computers run it. I don't like Microsoft as a company, they are dodgy fuckers, their near-monopoly was built on dirty tricks, and they will not hesitate to pull your pants down if they are given the advantage. Their mid-to-long term strategy over the past decade can be described as schizophrenic at best, playing catch up with whoever is in their sights that quarter. Nowadays I think very carefully before advocating any Microsoft solution, and their stuff ceased to be the centerpoint of my professional focus a good few years ago now. But they aren't going anywhere.

  • Mac OSX

I have the least experience with this platform of the three, but it's much nicer than Windows, with BSD underneath for the geeks. It's very responsive, and a joy to navigate.

For the most part, shit just works, and this is why Apple stuff is popular. But if it doesn't, or it doesn't work quite the way you want it to, you can easily find yourself shit out of luck. For instance, writing to NTFS volumes is a pain.

The biggest disadvantage is that it's only available on their hardware (unless you count Hackintosh, which is risky) so if their hardware doesn't meet your requirements, again you're shit out of luck. Which is pretty much the Apple philosophy - if you don't like it exactly the way we decide it to be (which may change at any time) then fuck you. This annoys me, as does the Apple reality distortion field. So many people will believe anything they say without question, it's really quite scary, almost like a religion. (Macs dont get viruses? Pull the other one ...)

  • Linux

I've been using Linux regularly on the desktop for about a decade, having occasionally flirted with it in the past. Servers, longer than that.

Desktop Linux is hamstrung by the same thing that gives it its lifeblood - diversity. When you walk into a restaurant and order a steak, most people aren't interested in the life story of the cow, don't want to cook it themselves, nor do they want to be asked more than the bare minimum of questions. Yet this is what desktop Linux is often like.

Which distro? Which desktop environment? LTS, 6-monthly dist-updates, rolling release or cutting edge? BIOS or UEFI? Would you like dual boot with that sir? Want to install that driver for your cheap-ass printer that they only started making a month ago? Well have fun pissing about with a "terminal" that looks like you just sneezed on your screen. You don't understand that? Well it's OK! The internet has your back! There are loads of internet forums and chat rooms where you too can ask for help and be condescended to by some needlessly aggressive fuckwit who will tell you in very undiplomatic terms that you shouldn't have bought that piece of shit printer in the first place, berate you for supporting the capitalist scumbags who manufactured it, and instead demand that you should adopt his exact workflow that doesn't involve printing in the first place, without any appreciation of what you're trying to accomplish. If you're lucky, another equally odious fool will step in, disagree with the first one, and you get a free nerd battle all for free! Hooray for the internet!

Normal humans, on the other hand, want shit that just works. I admit I over exaggerated the above, particularly in relation to the Linux community, in the interests of amusement, but you get my point. Desktop Linux however is getting better and better every day - just know that it's not really the no.1 thing Linux is about.

Software is sometimes thin on the ground, all the desktop environments lack a certain polish, graphics performance is sometimes not on-par with other platforms (because of the driver software) and if anything goes wrong with it, the number of people who can genuinely help you is far less than Windows. Some functions you would see a GUI for on Windows, you have to resort to the command line on Linux.

But you can do pretty much anything with it. My favourite, and most trusted machine is my Linux one. I do most of my work on Linux. It will sing and dance to your tune, is fast, reliable, and trustworthy. It has a lot of use-cases absolutely nailed. A lot of casual users of computers only use theirs for web browsing and email - for that kind of thing, Linux is ideal, and there are distros available that cater for casual users. Power users will feel right at home, as long as they don't rely on any software that is unavailable. Gamers are starting to get some love, with the release of Steam, and the gradual increase in quality of the graphics subsystem is great to see.

FYI, on the desktop, at the moment I am using Manjaro Linux with the KDE 5 desktop.

TL;DR: Use the right tool for the job.
